## The question

[How do I calculate $ \int_{1}^{3} x/(2-x) \;\mathrm{d}x$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1299698/how-do-i-calculate-int-13-x-2-x-mathrmdx), asked by [xsr](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/238869/xsr) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-05-26; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> $\int_{1}^{3} \frac{x}{2-x} \;\mathrm{d}x$
>
> $\int_{1}^{2} \frac{x}{2-x} \;\mathrm{d}x$ + $\int_{2}^{3} \frac{x}{2-x} \;\mathrm{d}x$
>
> $u = 2-x$
>
> $\lim_{e\to0} \left[  \int_{-e}^{1} \frac{2-u}{u} \;\mathrm{d}u +  \int_{-1}^{e} \frac{2-u}{u} \;\mathrm{d}u \right]$
>
> No matter what I do this is giving me 0, but the answer is -2.
:::

I guess from the start of your work that you are using the [Cauchy Principal Value][1] to work around the improperness of the integrals.  In that case, you've got the right idea.  After substituting $u=2-x$, $du =-dx$, you have
$$\int_1^3 \frac{x}{2-x}\,dx = \int_{-1}^1 \frac{2-u}{u}\,du = \int_{-1}^1 \frac{2}{u}\,du - \int_{-1}^1 1 \,du$$
Now show that the PV of $\int_{-1}^1 \frac{2}{u}\,du$ is zero and you are done.

  [1]: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_principal_value
